title: Quiz: Penalised Regression and Decision Trees

questions.text: Ridge regression minimises RSS + λΣβⱼ². What happens to the coefficients as λ → ∞?
options: All coefficients are set to exactly zero (variable selection occurs)
All coefficients shrink toward zero but remain non-zero — Ridge never sets a coefficient to exactly zero
The model becomes equivalent to OLS
Only the largest coefficient is affected
questions.explanation: As λ → ∞, the penalty dominates and all coefficients are driven toward zero. However, the L2 penalty (squared) has a smooth ball with no corners on the coordinate axes, so the minimum of RSS + λ||β||² always lies in the interior, never exactly on an axis. Ridge shrinks but does not select.

questions.text: LASSO can set some regression coefficients to exactly zero, performing automatic variable selection.
questions.explanation: The L1 penalty (sum of absolute values) creates a diamond-shaped constraint region with corners on the coordinate axes. The RSS contours tend to touch the constraint at a corner where one or more coordinates are exactly zero. This geometric property gives LASSO its variable selection capability.

questions.text: cv.glmnet() returns lambda.min and lambda.1se. In which situation would you prefer lambda.1se over lambda.min?
options: When you want the model with the lowest training error
When you want a more parsimonious model that is nearly as good as the minimum-CV model — one-SE rule sacrifices a little CV performance for fewer predictors
When the sample size is very large (n > 10,000)
When using Ridge (alpha = 0) rather than LASSO
questions.explanation: lambda.1se applies the one-standard-error rule: choose the most regularised (largest lambda) model whose CV error is within one SE of the minimum CV error model. This gives a sparser, more interpretable model at minimal cost in predictive performance. It is especially useful when interpretability matters.

questions.text: In a regression tree, the first split is on carat ≤ 1.0 vs carat > 1.0. What does this tell you?
options: Carat = 1.0 is the most common diamond size
Carat is the most important predictor — the split that reduces price variance most at the root
Diamonds weighing more than 1 carat are rare
The tree cannot use other predictors until carat is exhausted
questions.explanation: A regression tree greedily chooses the split that maximally reduces the residual variance at each step. If carat is the first split, it is the single predictor-threshold combination that explains the most variance in price — confirming carat as the dominant predictor.

questions.text: Why does the log-log OLS model typically have lower RMSE than a regression tree with maxdepth = 4 on the diamonds dataset?
options: OLS always has lower RMSE than trees on any dataset
The tree with maxdepth=4 has at most 16 leaf nodes — very coarse piecewise-constant predictions — while OLS captures the smooth continuous price-carat relationship
Trees are fitted by minimising MAE, not RMSE
OLS uses more predictors than the tree
questions.explanation: A tree with maxdepth=4 partitions the feature space into at most 2⁴ = 16 rectangular regions, predicting the mean price within each region. This is very coarse compared to the smooth, continuous OLS fitted surface. The tree's prediction surface is a staircase; OLS produces a smooth curve that fits the data more precisely.

questions.text: In glmnet, alpha = 0.5 fits an Elastic Net that uses a mixture of Ridge and LASSO penalties.
questions.explanation: The glmnet penalty is λ[α||β||₁ + (1−α)||β||₂²]. alpha = 0 is pure Ridge, alpha = 1 is pure LASSO, and intermediate values (0 < alpha < 1) are Elastic Net — combining the variable selection of LASSO with the grouping and stability of Ridge.
